title: New evidence undermines our theories of the universe
subtitle: Spinning galaxy observations suggest the universe itself is spinning
author: Lior Shamir
introduction: New observations appear to have undermined our leading theories of the universe — so claims Kansas State University computer scientist Lior Shamir, who has identified that far more spiral galaxies spin clockwise than counter-clockwise as seen from Earth. This is a near 50% asymmetry, visible to the naked eye. And it grows stronger the deeper into cosmic history we look. Under the cosmological principle, the century-old assumption that the universe looks the same from every vantage point, an observer anywhere should see a roughly even split. Shamir's data suggests otherwise, and the implications may require a whole new cosmological theory. Furthermore, the same systematic bias that could explain the spiral galaxy asymmetry may also be inflating the measurements behind two of cosmology's most stubborn open problems: dark energy, the unexplained force thought to be accelerating the universe's expansion, and the Hubble tension, the unresolved disagreement over how fast the universe is expanding.
body:
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is the most powerful astronomical imaging device ever built. With its ability to image the early universe, it provides observations that challenge our understanding of the cosmos, gradually leading to a new era in cosmology.

One of the unexpected observations made by JWST is the asymmetry between the number of galaxies that rotate in one direction and the number of galaxies that rotate in the opposite direction. That is, the number of galaxies imaged by JWST that rotate clockwise is not the same as the number of galaxies that rotate counterclockwise. That can be seen by observing spiral galaxies imaged by JWST deep field images.

Spiral galaxies such as our own Milky Way have arms, and the shape of these arms discloses the direction of rotation of the galaxy. JWST provides exceptionally sharp images of galaxies in the deep universe, and the highly detailed images allow us to identify their direction of rotation and count them. The JWST Advanced Deep Extragalactic Survey (JADES) is the largest deep field taken by JWST. Surprisingly, it shows 158 galaxies that rotate clockwise, and just 105 galaxies that rotate counterclockwise. That exhibits a very substantial difference of nearly 50%.

The recent tensions and observations that conflict with the standard cosmological theories, and even with themselves, reinforce the need to consider other explanations that are outside the standard cosmology.

In fact, the observation of asymmetry between the number of galaxies that rotate in opposite directions was initially made before JWST was launched. Studies with ground-based telescopes using analysis of millions of galaxies showed a slight asymmetry of 1%-2%. But these observations were made by galaxies that are relatively close to Earth. JWST shows that the magnitude of the asymmetry grows as the galaxies are more distant from Earth. That is, in the early Universe most galaxies rotated in the same direction, and the directions of rotation have been becoming more chaotic as the Universe gets older. Using the power of JWST, the asymmetry between the number of galaxies rotating in opposite directions can be observed even by just looking at the image with the unaided human eye.

Spiral galaxies are unique astronomical objects in the sense that the way they look is sensitive to the location of the observer. But under the current working assumption of the cosmological principle, the Universe is expected to be homogeneous, which means that we are expected to see the same universe regardless of the location of the observer. Therefore, under the current working assumption, the number of galaxies rotating in one direction as seen from Earth is expected to be the same (within statistical error) as the number of galaxies that rotate in the opposite direction. JWST shows otherwise, and that can be seen even by simple manual inspection of JWST deep field images.

Observations that violate the cosmological principle are no longer uncommon, and multiple such observations have been made in the past decade. But these observations mostly violate the anisotropy assumption of the cosmological principle. The anisotropy assumption means that the Universe is the same in every direction of observation. Several observations have been shown to conflict with that assumption; one of them is the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) radiation. But the difference between the number of galaxies that rotate in opposite directions also violates the homogeneity assumption. Because spiral galaxies look differently based on the location of the observer, they can be used to study the homogeneity assumption of the cosmological principle.

Rotating universe and black hole cosmology

One of the possible explanations is that the Universe was born rotating, and the direction of rotation of the galaxies was inherited from the direction of rotation of the Universe. In that case the early universe is expected to be highly homogeneous in the direction of rotation of galaxies, and the distribution of the directions of rotation becomes more chaotic as the Universe gets older and galaxies interact with each other.

The concept of a rotating universe is not new, and was proposed already in the 1940s by Kurt Godel. But observational indications to prove or disprove the concept are difficult to find, mainly because the Universe has no frame of reference it can be compared with. Even the contention that the Earth rotates took hundreds of years to prove, despite having the Sun, the Moon, and the stars as frames of reference. The Universe does not have a frame of reference, making it more difficult to prove or disprove its rotation. The unique nature of spiral galaxies allows us to use them as an indication of a rotating universe.

One of the cosmological theories that agrees with a rotating universe is black hole cosmology. According to black hole cosmology, the Universe is the interior of a black hole that exists in a parent universe. The theory was proposed in the 1970s and was based on the remarkable agreement between the radius of the Universe (the Hubble radius) and the radius of a black hole given the mass of the Universe (the Schwarzschild radius). It is also in agreement with observations that were made later, such as the accelerated expansion of the Universe, which, according to black hole cosmology, can be explained without the need to assume the existence of dark energy. Black hole cosmology also agrees with the contention of a Big Bang, as black holes are also born, often from the death of a massive star. Although it is not considered a “mainstream” cosmological theory, the recent tensions and observations that conflict with the standard cosmological theories, and even with themselves, reinforce the need to consider other explanations that are outside the standard cosmology.

Figure 1: The JADES deep field of JWST. The field show 158 spiral galaxies that rotate clockwise, while just 104 galaxies that rotate counterclockwise.

Effect of the rotation of the Milky Way galaxy

While the asymmetric distribution of spin directions of spiral galaxies can be a feature of the real Universe, there is also another option. The Milky Way galaxy rotates in velocity of approximately 220km/sec. The galaxies imaged by JWST have rotational velocity of their own. The rotational velocity of the galaxies that are observed relative to the rotational velocity of the Milky Way galaxy leads to a slight difference in their brightness. That happens due to the relativistic beaming effect. Galaxies that rotate in the opposite direction relative to the Milky Way are expected to be slightly brighter compared to galaxies that rotate in the same direction relative to the Milky Way.

Given the rotational velocities of the galaxies, the relativistic beaming effect is expected to be negligible. But it should also be remembered that the physics of galaxy rotation is one of the greatest mysteries in space science and is not yet fully understood. We do know that the rotation of galaxies does not follow the laws of “conventional” physics, leading to the theory of dark matter and other explanations designed specifically to address the provocative nature of galaxy rotation. Therefore, it is possible that the effect of galaxy rotation can be more substantial than expected according to theory.

Because galaxies that rotate in the opposite direction to the Milky Way are brighter than galaxies that rotate in the same direction relative to the Milky Way, we are supposed to see more galaxies that rotate in the opposite direction. That means that the number of galaxies in the Universe that rotate in one direction is the same as the number of galaxies rotating in the opposite direction. But because galaxies that rotate in the opposite direction relative to the Milky Way are brighter, we see more of them, and therefore an Earth-based observer is expected to see a different number of galaxies. That is what we see in the JWST deep fields.

If that is indeed the case, we expect to see the asymmetry peaks around the Galactic pole, where the rotational velocity of the Milky Way has full effect. At the same time, we expect to see no asymmetry around the Galactic plane, where the rotational velocity of the Milky Way has no effect compared to the observed galaxies. Observations using millions of galaxies show exactly that. The magnitude peaks around the poles of the Galaxy, and disappears around the Galactic plane. The same pattern is observed in the Northern and Southern ends of the Galactic pole, where both show exactly the same thing: Galaxies that rotate in the opposite direction relative to the Milky Way are more prevalent than galaxies rotating in the same direction relative to the Milky Way. The JWST JADES deep field that showed the high difference between the number of galaxies is close to the Southern Galactic pole, and therefore the differences are expected.

Figure 2: The differences in the number of galaxies with opposite directions of rotations in different parts of the sky as determined by 1.3 million galaxies imaged by DESI Legacy Survey. The observation shows that the asymmetry peaks in proximity to the Galactic pole (at 12o,-28o, and its opposite side at 192 o,28 o), and disappears in the Galactic plane.

An interesting observation is that experiments with tens of thousands of galaxies show that the difference in brightness increases when the galaxies are more distant from Earth. That observation can be important to understand several unsolved cosmological mysteries. One of these mysteries is the H0 tension. The H0 tension is the disagreement between the expansion rate of the Universe when determined using the cosmic microwave background radiation, and the expansion rate when determined using Type Ia supernovae. Each of these measurements shows a different expansion rate of the Universe. But because they both measure the same Universe, they are expected to be the same. It is clear that the Universe cannot have two different rates of expansion, and therefore at least one of these expansion rates is not fully accurate.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Cosmology in crisis With Claudia de Rham, George Ellis, Bjørn Ekeberg, Jay Shapiro

But if the brightness of astronomical objects is affected by their rotational velocity relative to the Milky Way, and the magnitude of the difference is a function of its distance from Earth, it can mean that the brightness of supernovae as observed from Earth is also affected. A Type Ia supernova is a special type of supernova whose absolute brightness is always the same. Therefore, its brightness as seen from Earth determines its distance, making it a very important distance candle in astronomy. The small brightness differences can lead to slightly different expansion rates, and therefore to a different expansion rate determined by the CMB, aka the H0 tension.

Indeed, this was observed using a relatively small set of Ia supernovae (a catalog called SH0ES) to determine the expansion rate of the Universe. When using only Ia supernovae in galaxies that rotate in the same direction relative to the Milky Way, the expansion rate determined using Ia supernovae is in very good agreement with the expansion rate determined from the CMB. On the other hand, using only galaxies that rotate in the opposite direction relative to the Milky Way makes the H0 tension larger.

The effect can also be related to other observations that rely on Ia supernovae as a reliable distance measurement, such as the mysterious accelerated expansion of the Universe. It is not yet entirely clear that the asymmetry observed from Earth is indeed driven by the difference in brightness of galaxies rotating in opposite directions. It is obviously still possible that the asymmetry is a feature of the real Universe. But if it is driven by the differences in brightness of galaxies rotating in opposite directions, the observation can provide the solution to several other puzzling tensions that currently do not have a proven explanation.
